item.title: A7 · What Actually Works? Housing Policy Options Compared
item.description:
1. One test, different clocks. Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake of the DIW, the German Institute for Economic Research, write that more social housing can bring improvement only in the medium to long run, while a higher Wohngeld relieves households quickly. Tighter rent controls might limit further increases, but they are not targeted support for the households under most strain. The political scientist Max-Christopher Krapp adds that the tools serve different goals, affordability, availability and access, which can conflict. A study of 77 large cities by Andrej Holm, Stephan Junker and Kevin Neitzel, funded by the trade-union-linked Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, looked at three of the four tools: Wohngeld, subsidised building and the rent brake. All three, it found, are "only very limited" help in closing the supply gap for low-income households, despite costing about four billion euros a year.
2. The rent brake: what it is. Since 2015 the Mietpreisbremse, the rent brake, has applied in designated tight markets. A new lease there may be at most 10 percent above the ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete, the local reference rent. Flats first let after 1 October 2014 are exempt, as are first lettings after a full modernisation and cases where the previous tenant paid more. The brake now runs to the end of 2029, and in January 2026 the Federal Constitutional Court upheld it, finding its alleged negative effects "not proven". In 2018 the brake applied in 313 of about 11,000 municipalities, home to almost 28 percent of the population. The business-funded German Economic Institute, the IW, counts 477 municipalities in 2024.
3. The rent brake: small and short-lived. DIW economists Kholodilin, Andreas Mense and Claus Michelsen found that the brake works only where new-lease rents had been rising by at least 3.9 percent a year. In those places rents fell once, by about 2.9 percent. New buildings, which are exempt, acted as a "pressure valve". Philipp Breidenbach, Lea Eilers and Jan Fries of the RWI estimate a 2.5 percent effect: about 12.50 euros a month less for a 60-square-metre flat in Berlin. The effect is larger at the cheap end, but it "does not change substantially" the situation of low-income tenants, and it disappears after about one to one and a half years. Enforcement is weak: in large cities with the brake, furnished and fixed-term flats grew from 15 to 35 percent of listings, which the authors suspect is an evasion route; in a Munich survey, 2.2 percent of respondents had challenged their landlord over an excessive rent.
4. Who gains from rent regulation. Mense, Michelsen and Kholodilin find that the brake mainly helps low-income households already inside regulated markets. It made finding a nearby flat easier for the lower three quarters of incomes, but caused misallocation even in the short run. Their 2018 DIW report had called it plausible that low incomes gain little, because landlords still pick other applicants, and middle incomes more. Pekka Sagner and Michael Voigtländer of the IW, writing for the liberal Friedrich Naumann Foundation, say older tenants and higher earners gain most, because they move less often. For existing contracts there is a separate cap, the Kappungsgrenze: rents may rise at most 20 percent in three years, or 15 percent in tight markets. Oliver Falck and colleagues at the ifo Institute credit it with keeping sitting tenants' rents moderate. In the seven largest cities, though, asking rents are 48 percent above existing rents.
5. The international evidence on rent control. Kholodilin's review of the empirical literature finds rent controls "quite effective" at slowing the rents they cover, but with "a wide range of adverse effects affecting the whole society". In San Francisco, Rebecca Diamond, Timothy McQuade and Franklin Qian found covered tenants nearly 20 percent more likely to stay, but landlords cut rental supply by 15 percent, raising rents city-wide by 5.1 percent. Catalonia's 2020 controls lowered rents by about 4 to 6 percent with no detectable fall in rental supply, according to Jordi Jofre-Monseny and colleagues (abstract only).
6. Social housing: built to expire. By the IW's count, Germany's social housing stock fell from 2.87 million flats in 1990 to 1.07 million in 2022, or 4.7 percent of rented flats. Rent and allocation caps typically end after 25 or 30 years. Holding the stock steady would take about 41,200 new caps a year, against about 21,600 built a year between 2018 and 2022. The Bundestag research service notes that courts accept only time-limited caps, of roughly 20 to 30 years. Internationally, Kholodilin, Sebastian Kohl and Florian Müller find that large sectors survived where dedicated social housing institutions existed. Holm and colleagues counted fewer than 5,000 new subsidised flats in the ten largest cities in 2014 against a gap of 880,000 low-income households, yet still call subsidy programmes the most reliable of the three tools for low incomes.
7. Who lives there, and do non-profits charge less? In survey data from around 2013, Michael Schier and Voigtländer of the IW found only about 46 percent of social housing households below the poverty line, a stricter test than the legal income limits. In big cities the IW found private landlords charging 8.70 euros per square metre, against 7.50 at cooperatives and 7.40 at municipal companies. Municipal companies alone did not raise rents significantly from 2013 to 2017, yet almost 30 percent of their tenants earn above the median. Matthias Wrede finds cooperative rents about 4 percent lower for comparable flats. A tighter Kappungsgrenze lowered rents at cooperatives and other non-profits, but not significantly at for-profit landlords. In Austria, Michael Klien and colleagues at the economic research institute WIFO estimate that a 10 percent higher share of non-profit housing lowers unregulated rents by 30 to 40 cents per square metre, about 5 percent (abstract only). Selim Banabak finds a similar pattern within Vienna (abstract only). US evidence cuts the other way: Todd Sinai and Joel Waldfogel find that, on average, three subsidised units displace two that the market would have built, though less in large markets.
8. Wohngeld: fast, but who does it reach? At the end of 2025, about 1.3 million households received Wohngeld, an average of 296 euros a month. It cost 4.99 billion euros, and in about half of recipient households a pensioner is the main earner. Fewer than one percent of recipients live in the most expensive rent band, the one that includes Munich, and almost 70 percent live in the three cheapest. When rent rises, the household bears about 40 percent of the increase itself. Earlier studies estimated that about half of eligible households do not claim; Wohngeld offices put the figure at 17 percent. Krapp links low take-up to little awareness and a cumbersome application.
9. Does Wohngeld end up with landlords? Gabrielle Fack found that in France each extra euro of housing benefit raised new claimants' rents by 78 cents (abstract only). After a Finnish reform in 2002, Aki Kangasharju found 60 to 70 cents passed on in the private sector and none in the municipal sector (abstract only). With register data on a 2015 Finnish reform, Essi Eerola and colleagues find about 3.6 cents per euro, "little or no effect". For Germany, Tim Clamor, Ralph Henger and Voigtländer of the IW, studying 36 cities for the federal research institute BBSR, found no detectable effect of the 2008–2009 increases on asking rents: the gain went entirely to recipients.
10. Building more: the numbers and the chains. Germany completed 206,600 flats in 2025, the fewest since 2012, taking 27 months from permit to completion. The IW puts need at 372,600 a year for 2021 to 2025. Using German data, Mense finds that one percent more new supply lowers rents by about 0.2 percent across the whole distribution, slightly less at the bottom. Each new flat frees about 4.8 second-hand flats. In Helsinki, moving chains from new market-rate flats quickly reach middle- and low-income neighbourhoods (abstract only). In four German cities, a BBSR study found chains of only 2.2 to 3.2 moves. Between 42 and 53 percent of vacated flats went to people moving in from elsewhere, and on re-letting, 30 percent of flats in Bremen and 65 percent in Leipzig moved up at least one price band.

item.title: A6 · Expropriation (Vergesellschaftung): Does It Work, and How?
item.description:
1. What Article 15 allows. Article 15 of the Grundgesetz, the Basic Law, lets land, natural resources and means of production be transferred "into common ownership or other forms of public enterprise" by a law that sets the type and amount of compensation. The Bundestag research service distinguishes this socialisation, Vergesellschaftung, from expropriation, Enteignung, under Article 14: expropriation takes a single asset for a public project, such as land for a motorway; socialisation moves whole enterprises or sectors into an economy run for public needs rather than profit. As of 2019 the power had never been used, and Berlin's 2026 framework law still calls it an instrument "so far not applied in practice". Compensation is required, so this is not confiscation. Whether it must equal market value is contested; one argument against full market value is that it would make socialisation practically impossible for lack of public money.
2. The 2021 referendum. The campaign Deutsche Wohnen & Co enteignen ("expropriate Deutsche Wohnen and Co") collected almost 360,000 signatures. Its ballot text asked the Senate, Berlin's government, to take all steps to socialise the holdings of every profit-oriented company with more than 3,000 flats in Berlin. Public companies and cooperatives were exempt. The flats were to go to an Anstalt öffentlichen Rechts (AöR), a public-law institution, run with majority participation of tenants, staff and city society, barred from reselling them, and paying compensation "well below market value". On 26 September 2021, turnout was 73.5 percent; 57.6 percent voted yes, 39.8 percent no and 2.6 percent cast invalid ballots. The sociologist Joanna Kusiak, who campaigned for it, gives 59.1 percent. The vote was a resolution, not a law, and was not legally binding.
3. How many flats, and at what price. The Senate's official estimate before the vote put it at about 243,000 flats and compensation of 28.8 to 36 billion euros, with another 1.5 to 1.9 billion in one-off costs and 100 to 340 million euros a year in subsidies beyond the rents. The campaign put compensation for about 200,000 flats at 7.3 to 13.7 billion euros. Economists at the DIW, the German Institute for Economic Research, now count 220,000 to 240,000 flats, a little over a tenth of Berlin's housing. The expert commission tied the size to need: about 855,000 Berlin households, every second one, qualified for a Wohnberechtigungsschein, the certificate needed to rent subsidised housing. Of the city's roughly 1.6 million rental flats, public companies owned 351,689 and cooperatives 188,392, together about a third. The commission argues that adding about 220,000 socialised flats would bring the total into the range of that need.
4. The expert commission. The Senate appointed thirteen experts in March 2022, chaired by the former federal justice minister Herta Däubler-Gmelin; they reported on 28 June 2023. The majority found that Berlin has the power to legislate here, because the federal level has not used its power over socialisation and tenancy law is a different subject. It found a socialisation law compatible with Article 15 and proportionate, and a transfer to an AöR acceptable if non-profit management is secured by law. Three members, Wolfgang Durner, the former constitutional judge Michael Eichberger and Christian Waldhoff, dissented: they gave property rights more weight and said proportionality could not be settled on what the commission knew. The commission also records that the Senate refused it land-register data needed to identify the affected companies.
5. Compensation: three positions. Most of the majority held that compensation could be based on the income from future non-profit management, on what the budget can afford, or on the value a property would have under regulation that requires no compensation. The rest of the majority took market value as the starting point but allowed caps and larger deductions than in an ordinary expropriation. The three dissenters said compensation must always start from market value, with deductions possible. Kusiak reads the majority's income-based model as very close to the campaign's own "fair rents model". For European human-rights law, the Bundestag research service notes that the Strasbourg court accepts compensation below full market value for large-scale economic or social reforms, while expropriating an individual tends to require full value.
6. The 2026 framework law. On 18 March 2026 Berlin passed a framework law for any use of Article 15. The IW, the German Economic Institute, attributes it to the CDU–SPD coalition. It socialises nothing itself: each case needs a separate law, which must show that ordinary regulation of property would not achieve the aim. Socialisation must be proportionate and must not lastingly and significantly restrict the state budget. Compensation must be "appropriate", with market value as the starting point. Disputes over the amount go to the civil courts, and the law enters into force 24 months after promulgation. The campaign called it insufficient and drafted its own law. It announced a second, legally binding referendum in September 2023, but none had taken place by July 2026. After Die Linke, the Left Party, won Berlin's election in September 2026, socialisation became a central issue in coalition talks.
7. What the price tags assume: projections. Every cost figure is a projection. Geraldine Dany-Knedlik, Konstantin Kholodilin, Alexander Kritikos and Alexander Kriwoluzky of the DIW model compensation of 8 to 29 billion euros, financed one fifth by the state at 4 percent and four fifths by loans to the AöR at 5 percent. At a rent of 8 euros per square metre, roughly today's level in these flats, compensation up to 13.5 billion pays for itself; at 21 billion the budget would pay about 366 million euros a year, at 29 billion about 791 million. Sebastian Dullien of the IMK, the Hans Böckler Foundation's macroeconomic institute, with Patrick Kaczmarczyk, Tom Krebs and Achim Truger, value about 210,000 flats at 13.5 billion euros from rents affordable for low and middle incomes. They project 543 million euros a year in net income against 345 million in debt service. The DIW team attributes most of the gap between studies to interest assumptions.
8. Berlin's buybacks: evidence. Berlin has already bought flats from the big landlords. In September 2021 three state-owned companies bought about 14,750 flats and 450 commercial units from Vonovia and Deutsche Wohnen for about 2.46 billion euros. The offer had been 20,000 flats, but not all could be run economically on social terms. The Senate said the price matched the earnings value, the companies borrowed the money, and the budget was not burdened. In April 2024 the state company HOWOGE bought 4,495 flats in Lichtenberg plus building land from Vonovia in a package worth about 700 million euros; the flats' average rent was 7.04 euros per square metre. Dolls and colleagues at the ifo Institute show that Vonovia and Deutsche Wohnen shrank their Berlin holdings, partly through these sales, while municipal companies expanded.
9. Vienna: the comparison everyone cites. Council housing makes up roughly a quarter of Vienna's dwellings (abstract only). Justin Kadi and Johanna Lilius find a "remarkable stability" of social housing in Vienna and Helsinki in size, privatisation and new building (abstract only). Selim Banabak finds that Viennese subdistricts with more limited-profit housing are more likely to have lower private-rent paths, more so on the periphery than in the centre (abstract only). The commission cites an Austrian study finding that non-profit housing also dampens rents overall. These studies describe large non-profit sectors; none of them studies socialisation.

item.title: A5 · The Berlin Mietendeckel: Economics and Aftermath
item.description:
1. What Berlin passed. The Act on Rent Limitation in Housing in Berlin, the MietenWoG Bln, became known as the Mietendeckel, the "rent lid". Berlin's parliament passed it on 30 January 2020 by 85 votes to 64, with one abstention. It took effect on 23 February 2020 and was meant to run for five years. As the Constitutional Court records, the Senate and parliament argued that the federal rent brake had not stopped rising rents and was often circumvented by side agreements. The law was to keep adequate housing available to middle- and low-income households in every part of the city.
2. Three rules. First, a freeze: no rent could exceed the rent agreed on 18 June 2019, the cut-off date. Second, ceilings for every new letting, taken from a table: from 3.92 to 9.80 euros per square metre of net cold rent, the rent before heating and service charges, depending on the building's age and on whether the flat had central heating and a bathroom; a flat built between 1919 and 1949 with both was capped at 6.27 euros. Third, from 23 November 2020, a rent more than 20 percent above the ceiling, adjusted for location, was banned as excessive. After a modernisation the rent could rise by at most 1 euro per square metre, and fines reached 500,000 euros. Social housing and flats first ready to live in from 1 January 2014 were exempt; Anja Hahn, Konstantin Kholodilin and Sofie Waltl of the DIW, the German Institute for Economic Research, put those newer flats at about 4 percent of Berlin's stock. They note that the ceilings came from Berlin's 2013 rent index, raised in line with real wages, and so lay far below market rents.
3. First- and second-generation control. The DIW team explains the distinction behind the debate. First-generation controls, like those of the two world wars, cap the rent itself, including for new tenants. Second-generation controls limit increases during a tenancy and leave the starting rent largely free. They call the Mietendeckel a return to the first generation. Germany knew such controls well: according to the Bundestag research service, controls on the rents of Berlin's older buildings ended only in 1987, with transition rules until 1994. In 1995 the economist Richard Arnott argued that economists' hostility to rent control rested on models of perfectly competitive markets and on the hard controls of post-war New York and Europe, and that the case against softer modern systems was weak (abstract only). Kholodilin's 2024 review of the empirical literature finds that rent controls are quite effective at slowing rent growth in controlled flats, but bring a wide range of adverse effects (abstract only).
4. The court ruling. The challenge came from 284 members of the Bundestag from the CDU/CSU and FDP, joined by referrals from two courts. In an order of 25 March 2021, published on 15 April, the Court's Second Senate declared the whole law void. It did not rule on whether the rents were fair. It ruled on who may legislate: rent levels in non-subsidised housing belong to civil law, a field shared with the federal level, and the federal government had already regulated them conclusively in sections 556 to 561 of the Civil Code, including the rent brake. That left no room for a state law. Berlin had argued that the 2006 federalism reform gave states power over "housing" and so over public-law price limits. A legal opinion for the Senate by Ulrich Battis had found the freeze defensible, but not the ceilings and rent reductions. The decision was unanimous in its result and seven to one on its reasoning.
5. What happened to rents. Hahn, Kholodilin and Waltl, later joined by Marco Fongoni, studied rental advertisements. Asking rents for regulated flats fell by 7 to 11 percent compared with unregulated ones as soon as the law took effect, yet only about a quarter of the adverts stated a rent that complied with it. Mathias Dolls, Clemens Fuest and colleagues at the ifo Institute compared Berlin with Germany's thirteen next-largest cities and found a two-tier market: rents for the exempt newer flats grew about 5 percentage points faster than elsewhere in 2020, and about 9 points faster in early 2021. In Potsdam, just outside the law's reach, asking rents rose by roughly 5, 9 and 12 percent over the first three quarters of 2020. In a survey of 283 private landlords, Pekka Sagner and Michael Voigtländer of the IW, the German Economic Institute, found that the average rent per square metre in their flats fell by 6 percent while the cap applied.
6. What happened to listings. New rental adverts halved, from more than 600 a week to fewer than 300. The ifo team found listings down by up to 60 percent, and they did not recover after the ruling: at the end of 2021, adverts for formerly regulated flats were about 70 percent below their 2017 level. Sagner and Voigtländer estimate that supply fell five times as much as rents (abstract only). Their survey adds a caveat: during the cap, landlords used online portals less, 54 instead of 64 percent, and personal networks more, 53 instead of 43 percent. So counts of online adverts overstate the fall in supply, while newcomers without contacts in Berlin found it harder to get a flat.
7. Shadow rents, conversions and building. Many landlords advertised two rents: the capped one, and a higher "shadow rent" to be paid, with arrears, if the law fell. Among covered adverts the share with two rents rose from 11 percent in February 2020 to 45 to 50 percent until March 2021, and the median shadow rent was 51 percent above the allowed one. Hahn and colleagues also cite official figures: conversions of rental flats into owner-occupied ones rose from 12,700 in 2019 to 19,200 in 2020, and completions of new flats fell by 14 percent in 2020 while rising almost 5 percent nationwide. The ifo team saw adverts for flats for sale rise while the cap applied and fall after it ended. Sagner and Voigtländer, by contrast, found no spillover on sale prices, which they read as investors waiting to see (abstract only).
8. The back payments. Once the law was void, tenants whose rents had been cut in November 2020, or who had signed shadow-rent contracts, could owe the difference. The Senate estimated that about 40,000 Berliners might need financial help. Benefit offices covered lawful claims for people on basic income support. Others, with incomes up to 280 percent of the federal income limit, 33,600 euros a year for a single person, could get an interest-free loan, the Sicher-Wohnen-Hilfe, from the state bank IBB. It could be turned into a grant if the tenant could not repay through no fault of their own. Vonovia waived back payments and Deutsche Wohnen offered instalments. Among private landlords surveyed after the ruling, 32 percent would demand the full amount without exceptions and 6 percent would waive it.
9. The rent brake, for comparison. Since 2015, the Mietpreisbremse, the federal "rent brake", has let states designate tight markets where a new tenancy may start at most 10 percent above the local comparative rent, the going rate for similar flats. Flats first used after 1 October 2014 are exempt. Kholodilin, Andreas Mense and Claus Michelsen found in 2018 that it can only bite where new-contract rents had been rising by more than 3.9 percent a year. There it slowed them, sometimes with a one-off fall of up to 2.9 percent, and it more likely encouraged than discouraged new building. Philipp Breidenbach, Lea Eilers and Jan Fries estimate an effect of only 2.5 percent, larger for cheaper flats and fading over time (abstract only). Mense, Michelsen and Kholodilin find that it raised rents in the free segment and reduced moving only among high-income households (abstract only). The Constitutional Court upheld the rent brake in 2019, and in January 2026 it rejected a complaint against the brake's extension and Berlin's ordinance. In December 2024 the federal government approved a draft to extend it to the end of 2029.

item.title: A4 · Investors and the City: Does More Investment Make Housing More Affordable?
item.description:
1. The great sell-off. Tobias Held of the BBSR, the federal institute for building and urban research, counts about 2 million flats that changed hands in 332 sales of 800 flats or more between 1999 and mid-2011. The federal government and the states sold 532,000 of them, municipalities 379,000, about one in seven municipal flats, and foreign financial investors bought about 56 percent of all flats traded. The largest municipal deals were Berlin's sale of its company GSW, about 65,700 flats, to Cerberus and Goldman Sachs in 2004, and Dresden's sale of its company WOBA, about 47,800 flats, to Fortress in 2006. Germany had no national privatisation law. The Bundestag research service names one exception: the Old Debts Assistance Act required former East German state housing companies to privatise 15 percent of their stock.
2. From private equity to the stock market. Gertjan Wijburg and Manuel Aalbers describe three waves: West German banks' failed attempt to liberalise housing finance after unification; the "financialised privatisation" of public housing by private equity firms and hedge funds from the late 1990s; and, after the global financial crisis, booming prices and listed real estate companies (abstract only). Vonovia is the clearest case. The British firm Terra Firma bought 64,000 railway workers' flats in 2001 through a company called Deutsche Annington, which went public in 2013 and was renamed Vonovia after taking over its rival Gagfah in 2015. Wijburg, Aalbers and Susanne Heeg call this a shift from "financialisation 1.0", pure speculation, to "2.0": long-term investment whose shares can still be traded short-term (abstract only). In autumn 2021, at its third attempt, Vonovia took over Deutsche Wohnen, a deal covering about 135,000 flats, the second-largest the BBSR has recorded since 1999.
3. Big, but not dominant. At the end of 2015 the nine larger listed housing companies owned about 890,000 flats, about 3.8 percent of all rental flats; Vonovia alone held almost 400,000. A BBSR study led by Stefan Kofner of the Zittau/Görlitz University of Applied Sciences found their flats concentrated in larger cities and particular neighbourhoods, many of them current or former social housing, with the largest shares in Berlin, North Rhine-Westphalia and Saxony. All private housing companies together, listed or not, owned 3.5 million rental flats in the 2022 census. When Vonovia and Deutsche Wohnen merged, the Federal Cartel Office judged the rental market still fragmented, with municipal companies, cooperatives and private landlords limiting Vonovia's room to act, as the Bundestag research service records.
4. Rents after the sales. The first studies, summarised by the Bundestag research service, found little harm. A 2007 federal study found rents in privatised stocks moving with the market, with luxury modernisation the exception. Dominik Weiß, using the Socio-Economic Panel household survey, found that rents of privatised flats rose 11.8 percent from 1999 to 2006: more than in municipal flats, but less than in rented flats on average. Andrej Holm warned that such early studies could not support firm long-term conclusions. From 2010 to 2015, Vonovia's average net cold rent, the rent before heating and utilities, rose 13.6 percent and the GSW's 19.6 percent. Companies in the GdW, the federal housing association that includes municipal companies and cooperatives, raised theirs by 10.3 percent, and the national rent index rose 6.7 percent.
5. How rents go up. In a 2025 BBSR survey of 26 private housing companies with over 900,000 flats, more than half of all tenancies had a rent increase between 2019 and 2021. Forty-two percent were raised towards the local comparative rent, the going rate for similar flats, and 11 percent through a modernisation surcharge. The surcharges were larger: on average 81 cents per square metre a month, against 33 cents. The companies raised rents more regularly than private individual landlords.
6. The modernisation surcharge. Under section 559 of the Civil Code, a landlord who modernises a flat may add 8 percent of the cost to the annual rent. Until the end of 2018 it was 11 percent. Repair costs and public subsidies must be deducted, and the rent may rise by at most 3 euros per square metre within six years, or 2 euros if it was below 7 euros. A flat modernised for at least a third of the cost of a comparable new build also escapes the rent brake for new leases. Ralph Henger of the IW, the German Economic Institute, which is financed by about 110 business and employers' associations, points out that the surcharge depends on cost, not on the energy saved. In his worked example with Leo Reutter, insulating walls and replacing windows costs 15,000 euros for an 80 square metre flat. The cold rent rises by 1.25 euros per square metre a month, while heating costs fall by 76 cents.
7. Who modernises, and who raises rents. In a 2010 survey of 1,301 energy retrofits by the state bank KfW and the IW, Henger and Michael Voigtländer found median rent rises of 28.6 percent at private companies, 25 percent at cooperatives and 5 percent at small private landlords. Only 88 of the cases were private companies. Kofner's team found that most listed companies spent less than the municipal average, mainly on routine maintenance, with large differences between firms. Vonovia's spending on maintenance and modernisation rose from about 11 euros per square metre in 2009 to 33 in 2015, and the companies expect a return of 6 to 8 percent on capital spent on modernisation. Between 2019 and 2021, private companies energy-retrofitted 12 percent of their flats, more often than individual landlords do.
8. Buying flats, not building them. The listed companies grew mainly by buying. Unlike municipal companies, only a few of them built. From 2019 to 2021 the stock of the very largest private companies grew by just over 3 percent, mostly through purchases of existing flats, and the companies named high construction costs as the main obstacle to building.
9. What new building does further down the market. Andreas Mense of the IAB, the Federal Employment Agency's research institute, uses weather delays in German construction as a natural experiment. One percent more new housing lowers average local rents by about 0.2 percent, at the cheap end too, and each new flat brings about 4.8 second-hand flats onto the rental market as people move up. The effect is as strong in booming markets. In Helsinki, Cristina Bratu, Oskari Harjunen and Tuukka Saarimaa find that such chains of moves quickly reach low-income neighbourhoods (abstract only). In the United States, Brian Asquith, Evan Mast and Davin Reed find that large new buildings in low-income areas lower nearby rents by about 6 percent (abstract only).
10. Jobs, wages and rents. Richard Hornbeck and Enrico Moretti study US cities whose factories become more productive. Each 1 percent of productivity growth raises rents by 1.47 percent. In the long run renters' purchasing power rises 0.62 percent, homeowners' 1.11 to 1.60 percent. In Germany, under half of households owned their home at the 2011 census.

item.title: A3 · Why Rents Rose: Structural Causes vs Corporate Greed
item.description:
1. How much rents rose. Konstantin Kholodilin and Malte Rieth of DIW Berlin, the German Institute for Economic Research, use data from the property association IVD. They find that net cold rents, the rent before heating and utilities, rose by about 70 percent on average from 2010 to 2025, by about 4 percent in 2025 alone and by up to 8 percent in the largest cities. Over the same period building land became about 104 percent dearer and owner-occupied flats 116 percent. The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, reports that new-contract rents in apartment buildings rose 6.3 percent in 2023.
2. More people, almost all from abroad. Germany's population has grown by about 225,000 a year since 2010. Deaths have exceeded births every year since 1972, so all of that growth comes from net immigration, which averaged about 345,000 a year from 1991 to 2024. The Bundesbank's models trace the price boom of the 2010s mainly to supply and demand, with income growth that also reflects strong labour-market immigration from 2011 to 2019, and find little evidence of destabilising speculation. Migration does not push rents in only one direction, though. Kathleen Kürschner Rauck and Michael Kvasnicka find that the 2015 refugee arrivals slowed rent growth in the counties that received them, apparently because residents saw the refugees as a drawback of the area. In an earlier version of the study, one percentage point more refugees went with advertised rents about 0.6 to 1 percent lower in the months after arrival (abstract only).
3. Too little building. Completions rose from 159,000 flats in 2009 to 306,400 in 2020, stayed at about 294,000 a year from 2021 to 2023, and fell to 206,600 in 2025, the lowest since 2012, according to Destatis, the Federal Statistical Office. The German Economic Institute (IW) puts the need at 372,600 new flats a year for 2021 to 2025. Even Munich, the best performer among the seven largest cities, built only 93 percent of what it needed. The need itself is contested: a rival forecast by the consultancy empirica put it at about 170,000 a year, mainly because it assumes lower immigration, and the IW stresses that all such figures rest on strong assumptions. By the end of 2024 only 2.2 percent of flats were empty and ready to let.
4. Building cost more. Destatis reports that prices for new residential buildings, counting only the building and not the land, rose 89 percent from 2010 to 2025, while consumer prices rose 38 percent. The Bundesbank links weak supply in 2023 to dearer materials, shortages, higher construction wages and tighter financing. Kholodilin and Rieth add a wave of construction insolvencies.
5. Land, the quiet driver. Across 14 rich countries, the economists Katharina Knoll, Moritz Schularick and Thomas Steger find that rising land prices, not building costs, explain about 80 percent of the rise in house prices since 1950. Germany was their outlier, with the weakest long-run increase: real house prices fell by about 0.8 percent a year from the 1980s to 2012. The Bundesbank finds that land prices rose faster than construction costs in the 2010s, and that more designated building land would damp prices.
6. Interest rates cut both ways. Martin Groiss and Nicolas Syrichas study 35 million German property listings from 2007 to 2023. Looser monetary policy raised prices strongly and rents more modestly, and widened the gap between them (abstract only). When rates rose from mid-2022, the Bundesbank says, buying became unaffordable for many and would-be buyers were pushed into renting, one reason for the jump in new-contract rents. Mortgage rates of about 3.8 percent in late 2025 are far above the 2012 to 2022 level, when real rates, after inflation, were close to zero.
7. Rigid supply, and the rules. In a paper for the Ruhr Economic Papers series, Eyayaw Beze estimates that German housing supply responds weakly to prices: from 2008 to 2019 house prices rose 26.6 percent and housing supply 6.7 percent. He had no data on land-use rules. Sebastian Eichhorn and David Pehlke find that strict regional planning reduces construction somewhat, but does not raise land prices or rents (abstract only). The Bundesbank says it cannot measure how far red tape, fixed land-use plans or local opposition held back building land.
8. Social housing leaving its caps. German social housing rests on a trade: cheap public loans in return for rent and tenant caps that end once the loans are repaid. Wolfgang Kiehle, writing in the political-system handbook of the Federal Agency for Civic Education, calls it a time-limited compromise. Private landlords received such subsidies too. German cities' social housing shares fell from over 30 percent in the 1980s to under 10 percent as flats passed to the market once their mortgages were paid off, according to Kholodilin, Sebastian Kohl and Florian Müller. The 1990 tax reform abolished the non-profit housing law, under which recognised companies capped dividends at 4 percent and charged rents that covered costs. The Bundestag research service records the official reason: the tax breaks were no longer needed and were poorly targeted. By an IW estimate, the stock of capped flats fell from 2.87 million in 1990 to 1.07 million in 2022, by about 33,000 a year until a 2002 reform and by 74,000 a year since. Caps typically run 25 or 30 years.
9. Who owns the flat. In household survey data for cities of over half a million people, Michael Voigtländer and Pekka Sagner of the IW find that municipal landlords' median rent stayed at about 7.40 euros per square metre from 2013 to 2017, while private housing companies' rose from 7.70 to 8.70 euros. They conclude that private landlords realised the profit potential that scarcity offered. The figures are not adjusted for location or quality. Direct tests of landlord market power come only from abroad in the sources I read. In New York, C. Luke Watson and Oren Ziv find that markups, the share of rent above cost, make up nearly a third of rents in Manhattan.

item.title: A2 · Who Pays the Price? Rising Rents and Low- and Middle-Income Households
item.description:
1. The load sits at the bottom. Eurostat's 2025 figures show 11.2 percent of people in Germany living in households that spend more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing, against 7.7 percent in the EU. In the poorest income fifth the share is 31.5 percent, in the second fifth 12.1 (EU: 7.1), in the middle fifth 7.0 (EU: 3.3), and in the top two fifths 3.8 and 1.5. This overburden rate counts total housing costs, including heating and utilities, after housing benefit is deducted, so it is not last episode's rent burden. On average, people living alone put 33.2 percent of disposable income into housing costs and single parents 31.7, against 21.3 for two adults without children; Destatis warns that the 2020 survey change rules out comparison with earlier years and the 2023 change in the owner questions limits it.
2. What is left after rent. Andrej Holm's team at Humboldt University used the 2018 Mikrozensus, the household survey, for 77 large cities and measured the income left after rent including utilities and heating. Households below the poverty threshold, under 60 percent of the median income, had on average 506 euros a month left; households above 140 percent of the median had 3,372 euros. Of households at 60 to 80 percent of the median, 69.8 percent paid more than 30 percent of their income, as did 63.5 percent of single parents and 62.1 percent of people living alone. Of the more than a million households left below the basic benefit rate, about 450,000 live on transfers alone and about 630,000 have earnings of their own.
3. Savings and wealth. The economists Christian Dustmann, Bernd Fitzenberger and Markus Zimmermann followed household budgets from 1993 to 2013. In the poorest fifth, housing's share of income rose from 27 to 39 percent, the average savings rate fell from 2 percent to minus 1 percent, and the share with any positive savings fell from 64 to 53 percent. Their sample includes owners. Median net wealth is 16,200 euros for renter households and 364,800 euros for owner-occupiers, according to the Bundesbank, which says age, household size and income explain part of the gap. Markus Grabka and Christoph Halbmeier of DIW Berlin add that a mortgage forces owners to build wealth through repayments, while renters face no such compulsion.
4. Tenant poverty and exposed groups. In the SOEP household panel, the share of tenants below 60 percent of median income, before housing costs, rose from about 16 percent in the early 1990s to just under 29 percent in 2015, while owners stayed near 4 percent. The authors count owners' saved rent as income and tie part of the rise in poverty risk across the whole population to newly arrived migrants. Among households aged 65 and over, 38 percent of tenants spent more than 40 percent of income on housing in 2016, against about a fifth in 1996. Students with their own household spent 54 percent of disposable income on housing in 2025, against 24 percent for the whole population, and 65 percent were overburdened. In big cities, households with a migration background lived on 34 square metres per person against 50 for others, yet paid a slightly higher share of income.
5. Cramped and cold. By the Eurostat definition, 11.7 percent of people in Germany lived in overcrowded homes in 2025, up from 10.2 percent in 2020, against 16.8 percent in the EU. The rate is 18.3 percent for market-rent tenants but under 4 percent for owners, 27.4 percent below the poverty line, and 46.7 percent for poor children. Sebastian Kohl and colleagues, funded by the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, find that overcrowding has risen since 2012 and that urban tenants' floor space per person stagnated or fell, but that once children and migration background are controlled, economic factors explain relatively little. In 2025, 5.7 percent of people could not keep their home adequately warm, 12.6 percent below the poverty line, and 4.6 percent were in arrears on utility bills, 8.0 percent below it; these series do not split by tenure, so they show no direct link to rent.
6. Lock-in. Niklas Gohl asked whether tenants paying far below the market rent stay put. In SOEP data for 2012 to 2016, private tenants with a rent discount of at least 30 percent, living where rents rose more than 4 percent a year, were about 3 percentage points less likely to move than other private tenants, who moved about 10 percent of the time each year. The gap was wider for low-income tenants and for those who were dissatisfied or found the flat too small. With person-level fixed effects the main estimate falls to 1.7 points, and Gohl stresses that the design is not causal and the data do not show whether people wanted to move.
7. Displacement and segregation. Fabian Beran and Henning Nuissl surveyed more than 2,000 Berlin tenants who had recently moved: more than 15 percent had been directly displaced, most often through a rent increase after refurbishment or a sale (abstract only). Marcel Helbig and Stefanie Jähnen of the WZB Berlin Social Science Center studied 74 cities to 2014. The share of benefit recipients who would have had to move for an even spread across neighbourhoods rose from 24.0 percent in 2005 to 26.6 percent in 2014, and 36 cities have neighbourhoods where over half of the children live on such benefits. Yet higher average rents did not increase segregation. A federal study of twelve quarters in nine cities found displacement of older people and of people starting families, but also that student flat shares compete well, so a simple story of rich replacing poor is too narrow.
8. Social housing today. There is no official count of social rental flats. A Länder-based estimate puts them at 2.87 million in 1990 and 1.07 million in 2022, about 4.7 percent of rented homes. The rent and occupancy caps typically last 25 or 30 years, and holding the stock level would take about 41,200 new caps a year to 2035, against about 21,600 social rental flats built a year in 2018 to 2022. DIW Berlin's Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake report that since 2002 the share of tenants spending over 40 percent of income on rent has exceeded the share living in social housing, and in 2021 it was almost twice as high. A comparison of up to 48 countries finds Germany's 76 percent fall from its peak the steepest in the West. Why the stock shrank belongs to the next episodes.
9. Wohngeld, the housing benefit. Wohngeld goes to lower-income households that do not receive basic income support. Its amount depends on household size, countable income and rent, rising with rent and falling with income, and rent counts only up to a ceiling set by the local rent level, one of seven Mietenstufen. The 2023 reform, Wohngeld-Plus, widened eligibility and added a heating-cost and a climate component. Recipient households rose 80 percent, from about 651,800 at the end of 2022 to about 1.17 million a year later, and reached about 1.3 million at the end of 2025, or 3.2 percent of households, at an average of 296 euros a month; in 51 percent the main earner is a pensioner. In 2024 fewer than 1 percent of recipient households lived in the highest rent level, which includes Munich, and about 70 percent in the lowest three. How many eligible households never claim is unsettled: a simulation for the federal institute BBSR found just under half before the reform, local offices guessed 17 percent, and an ifo paper cites a review giving 56 to 87 percent.
10. Basic income support and rent. Under Bürgergeld, the basic income support, "appropriate" housing costs are paid in full, and in the first twelve months the rent is not checked, as the Institute for Employment Research (IAB) described the rules in 2023. Where rent exceeds the local limit, households must cut costs, move or pay the difference from their standard allowance, unless a hardship exception applies; in a 2016 survey of local offices these covered 10.4 percent of households over the limit under SGB II, the system for jobseekers, and 34.4 percent under SGB XII, which covers older people and those unable to work. In the IAB's example of two fictional single people earning about 2,000 euros gross, roughly 1,150 euros remain after housing costs in Gera but about 900 in Munich, even with Wohngeld.

item.title: A1 · Can People Still Afford Rent? Then vs Now
item.description:
1. Three yardsticks, not one. The rent burden (Mietbelastung) is gross cold rent, meaning the basic rent plus the service charges paid to the landlord but not heating, as a share of household net income. Social scientists and property experts usually treat a burden above 30 percent as problematic, a rule of thumb rather than a measured boundary. The overburden rate used by Eurostat and the OECD counts people in households that spend more than 40 percent of disposable income on housing; in its wider version, housing costs also include utilities, maintenance and taxes. The third yardstick is residual income: what is left after housing costs, compared with the subsistence minimum. One research paper on German rent burdens puts it plainly: affordability cannot be measured directly, so rent-to-income ratios serve as a measurable indicator.
2. The official snapshot for 2022. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), tenant households spent on average 27.9 percent of their net income on gross cold rent, at 8.60 euros per square metre. In the first results, about 3.1 million households, 16 percent of tenant households, paid 40 percent or more. There is a catch for any "then versus now" question. Since the 2020 redesign of the Mikrozensus, the household survey behind these numbers, Destatis says 2022 cannot be compared with earlier years.
3. The long-run trend: up, then flat. Using the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), a household survey run since 1984, the DIW Berlin economists Konstantin Kholodilin and Pio Baake find that the burden rose in the early 1990s, has been roughly constant since about 2005, and has slipped slightly since 2015. In East Germany it jumped from about 4 percent in 1990 to about 25 percent in 2001, after rents frozen since 1936 were liberalised. Backhaus, Gebers and Schröder found the same shape: a substantial rise in the 1990s, then a relatively constant decade. Kholodilin and Baake name rising incomes, the rent brake (Mietpreisbremse, introduced in 2015 for new lettings in tight markets) and fewer moves as possible reasons for the recent slight fall, but say their data cannot show how much the brake mattered.
4. Rents against incomes. Asking rents, the rents advertised for new lettings, rose about 55 percent between 2010 and 2022, and about 70 percent in cities above 500,000 people. Rents in existing tenancies rose only about 19 percent. Over a shorter window, an Institut der deutschen Wirtschaft (IW) short report by Ralph Henger found that rents in multi-family buildings rose 10.2 percent from 2010 to 2016 while disposable household income rose 11.5 percent. Niklas Gohl, citing federal data, puts the rise for new contracts between 2010 and 2015 at about 18 percent nationally and 26 percent in big cities.
5. Sitting tenants versus newcomers. The federal research institute BBSR reports that in 2025 the average asking rent for a re-letting was 11.11 euros per square metre, against an estimated 7.76 euros for existing contracts: about 43 percent higher. Growth in asking rents slowed from 5.7 percent in 2023 to 4.8 and then 3.5 percent in 2024 and 2025. BBSR's explanation is that most flats are let long-term, and increases in running contracts are infrequent and legally limited. Gohl describes those limits as of 2019: a cap of 20 percent in three years, or 15 percent where states have designated tight markets. The size of the gap depends on the yardstick. BBSR's asking rents come from online adverts and its existing-rent figure is an estimate, while the IW found an average premium for new contracts of 14 percent in 2016 to 2018.
6. Newcomers: a third more per square metre, but a smaller gap in burden. In 2022 the average burden by move-in year was 26.9 percent before 1999, 27.3 percent for 1999 to 2008, 27.1 percent for 2009 to 2018, and 29.6 percent for 2019 or later. Recent movers pay 9.70 euros gross cold per square metre against 7.30 for pre-1999 tenants, about a third more, yet their burden is only about three points higher. The table does not say why. The IW reported that new tenants lived in somewhat less space per person than sitting tenants, 45.6 against 49.5 square metres in 2018.
7. Income is the sharpest divide. In 2022, households with under 1,500 euros net a month spent 44.6 percent of income on gross cold rent; households with 4,000 euros or more spent 15.9 percent. Households of four or more people under 1,500 euros spent 58.0 percent. Single-person households averaged 32.7 percent, two-person households 22.8 percent. Over time, Kholodilin and Baake find that the poorest fifth of tenants went from about 24 percent in 1990 to about 36 percent in 2021, while the richest fifth paid about 22 percent. Dustmann, Fitzenberger and Zimmermann, using a different survey and counting owners too, find that the bottom fifth's share of income spent on housing rose from 27 percent in 1993 to 39 percent in 2013, while the top fifth's fell from 16 to 14 percent.
8. Place matters, but less than income. In 2022 the burden was 29.0 percent in large cities, 27.7 percent in medium-sized towns and 26.0 percent in small towns and rural areas. Gross cold rent averaged 9.60 euros per square metre in large cities, and 11.00 euros for those who moved in from 2019. The burden for large-city newcomers was 30.9 percent. The spread by city size is far narrower than the spread by income. Asking rents in 2025 ranged from 21.01 euros in Munich to 8.64 in sparsely populated rural districts, and below 6 euros in parts of Saxony and Thuringia. Kholodilin and Baake find burdens lower in the East, with the statistical region of Chemnitz at 21.6 percent and the Cologne administrative district at 30.7 percent. The IW calculated, for new-contract rents, how much space a single median earner can rent for a quarter of net income: 36.2 square metres in Munich, 57.3 in Düsseldorf. Between 2018 and 2021, affordability fell in about three quarters of districts.
9. Germany in Europe: bad or good, depending on the yardstick. In 2025, 11.2 percent of Germany's population lived in households overburdened by housing costs, against 7.7 percent for the EU. The rate was 9.0 percent in 2020 and peaked at 13.0 percent in 2023; Destatis notes that figures from 2020 on are not comparable with earlier years because of a survey break, and that changed questions for owners in 2023 limit comparison with earlier years. Among people at risk of poverty the rate was 35.0 percent in 2025. Yet the OECD lists Germany among just five countries where fewer than half of low-income tenants in the private market are overburdened when total housing costs are counted. Germany also has the highest tenant share in the EU, with 52.8 percent of the population renting.
10. Residual income tells a related story. A Humboldt University team (Andrej Holm and colleagues), funded by the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung, used the 2018 Mikrozensus for 77 large cities. They found 12.9 percent of tenant households, about 1.1 million, had less than the subsistence minimum left after paying rent including utilities. The top income class had 4.4 times the net income of the bottom class before rent, and 6.7 times after it. A study of Berlin, Cologne and the Ruhr area from 2002 to 2018 by Marco Schmandt points the other way in aggregate: residual income rose along the whole distribution in two of the three markets despite real rent increases, largely because of changes in who lives there (abstract only).
